extracted.subtask_description: A multi-week undergraduate course project with exercises on Cantor's transfinite cardinals, countability proofs (bijections and diagonalization), and Veblen's algebraic/topological formulation of graphs (incidence matrices, circuits, mod-2 linear algebra). Includes instructor notes and hands-on matrix/graph computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Cantor in your own words
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain in your own words what Cantor means in the above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear interpretation of Cantor's statements (as given in the quoted passage). Relate phrases to modern terminology where helpful and justify your interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify equal cardinality via bijection (P vs N)
rubrics_metrics.description: From Cantor’s statement above, do P (set of perfect squares) and N (set of natural numbers) have the same cardinality? Justify your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a 1-1 correspondence (bijection) between the two sets or give a rigorous argument showing such a bijection exists (e.g., n ↦ n^2 or its inverse). Explicitly state the map and verify injectivity and surjectivity as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify equal cardinality via bijection (N vs Z)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Z denote the set of all integers. Do N and Z have the same cardinality? Justify your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an explicit bijection between N and Z (or a standard enumerative argument). Show how each integer is assigned a unique natural number (and vice versa) and explain why the mapping is one-to-one and onto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate Cartesian product N × N (countability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do N and N×N have the same cardinality? Justify your answer. Hint: Draw a picture of N×N and label each element by a unique natural number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an explicit enumeration/bijection (e.g., diagonal argument, pairing function, Cantor pairing function) mapping each pair (n,m) to a unique natural number. A pictorial grid with a traversal order may be used; explain why the traversal hits every pair exactly once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show Q is countable (cardinality of rationals)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the cardinality of Q (rationals)? Justify your answer. Hint: Establish a 1-1 correspondence between Q and (a subset of) Z×N and modify your solution to (8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate an enumeration or bijection of rational numbers (e.g., enumerate pairs (a,b) with gcd=1 and b>0, avoid duplicates or map to canonical reduced form). Use previous N×N enumeration and handle signs/zero appropriately; explain removal of repeats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern formulation of Cantor's < relation between cardinals
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe in modern terminology when two cardinals a and b are in the relation a < b, based on Cantor's quoted conditions (a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate Cantor's conditions into modern set-theoretic language (existence of an injection from M to N but no bijection, or existence of proper subset N1 of N equinumerous with M). Clarify equivalences and any assumptions (e.g., using injections/surjections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove transitivity of cardinal inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove Cantor's claim: if a < b and b < c, then a < c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the definitions of '<' in terms of injections/bijections or proper subset equivalences to show transitivity. Provide a clear chain of function constructions or contradiction argument as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aleph-zero greater than any finite number
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove Cantor's claim that ℵ0 (aleph-zero) is greater than any finite number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that ℵ0 (cardinality of N) is strictly larger than any finite cardinal by demonstrating there is no bijection between a finite set and N; or exhibit an injection from any finite n into N but not conversely.

rubrics_metrics.name: ℵ0 is least transfinite cardinal
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove Cantor's claim: ℵ0 is the least transfinite cardinal number. If a is any transfinite cardinal number different from ℵ0, then ℵ0 < a. Hint: Let a = |A|. Can you define a 1-1 map from N into A?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an injection from N into any infinite set A (e.g., choose distinct elements iteratively) and argue there cannot be bijection from A to N when A's cardinal is larger; discuss reliance on choice-like selection if needed (shadow of axiom of choice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor diagonalization to show [0,1] uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that ℵ0 < [0,1]. Outline Cantor’s diagonalization method by representing reals in [0,1] as infinite decimals (not ending in repeating 9's), enumerating them, and constructing a new decimal differing on the nth digit from the nth listed number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Cantor's diagonal argument: assume enumeration exists, build b with b_n ≠ a_nn for each n to get a real not in enumeration. Address decimal representation subtleties (avoid 0.4999… vs 0.5000…). Conclude [0,1] is uncountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reals strictly larger than countable
rubrics_metrics.description: Is R strictly greater than ℵ0? Justify your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend the [0,1] uncountability to all reals R by mapping or containment arguments (|R| = |[0,1]|). Provide a clear justification using bijections or injections/surjections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set strictly larger than set (Cantor's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove P(M) > M for any set M. Employ a generalized diagonalization method. Assume that M maps 1-1 onto P(M) and derive contradiction by considering the set N = { m in M : m ∉ f(m) } not in the range of f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present Cantor's diagonal argument for power sets: given any function f : M → P(M), construct N as above and show no m can map to N, producing contradiction; conclude no surjection exists from M onto P(M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce infinite increasing sequence of transfinite cardinals
rubrics_metrics.description: Using previous exercise, give an infinite increasing sequence of transfinite cardinal numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the power-set operation iteratively (M, P(M), P(P(M)), ...) or aleph hierarchy to produce strictly increasing sequence; justify strictness at each step via Cantor's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate topological '0-cell'/'1-cell' to graph terms
rubrics_metrics.description: In graph terminology, what is a '0-cell'? What is a '1-cell'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify 0-cells with vertices and 1-cells with edges in graph-theoretic language; explain ends/boundary relationships and how sets of cells correspond to subgraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent vertex/edge sets as binary symbols and define mod-2 addition
rubrics_metrics.description: Any set of 0-cells or 1-cells may be denoted by a symbol .x1; x2; ...;, where xi = 1 if the cell is in the set and xi = 0 otherwise. The sum (mod 2) of two such symbols is defined as symmetric difference (cells in exactly one set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use binary tuples to represent sets and define addition modulo 2 as set symmetric difference. Prove algebraic properties (e.g., if two sets each contain an even number of 0-cells, their sum contains an even number). Provide formal proof and set interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct H0 matrix for components
rubrics_metrics.description: Define H0: rows correspond to connected sub-complexes (components) and contain 1s for vertices in the component, 0s otherwise. For connected complexes H0 is one row of all 1s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label 0-cells and organize components to form block rows of 1s. For given graphs (G1, G2) construct H0 explicitly and explain why vertex-labeling assumption is an isomorphism-invariant choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct incidence matrix H1 and its properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Define H1 as the α0×α1 incidence matrix with entry (i,j)=1 iff vertex a0_i is incident with edge a1_j; each column contains exactly two 1's (both ends of each edge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a graph, build H1 accordingly (e.g., for G3). Use the column-two-ones property to check validity and to construct a graph from a suitable 0/1 matrix. Explain why some matrices cannot be incidence matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain limitations of incidence matrices for isomorphism testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why isomorphic graphs do not necessarily have the same incidence matrix and whether incidence matrices can be used to determine graph isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss dependence on vertex/edge ordering (permutations of rows/columns) and how relabelings correspond to permutation-similarity of matrices. Describe that while incidence matrices are not canonical, permutation equivalence can be used in principle; discuss computational issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block-diagonal form of H1 for disconnected graphs and R0 relations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graph with R0 connected components, H1 can be arranged as block-diagonal with non-zero blocks for each component. Adding rows of any block yields zero (mod 2) in every column; there are exactly R0 linearly independent relations among the rows of H1, so rank(H1) = α0 - R0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrate by finding H1 for given disconnected graphs (G1, G2), identify the R0 relations (sums of rows of each block), and verify the rank relation by reducing the matrix (mod 2). Note: reduce by hand mod 2 rather than using floating-point matrix utilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define one-dimensional circuit (1-circuit) and even-degree characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: A 1-circuit is a connected linear graph where each vertex is incident with exactly two 1-cells (edges). A linear graph decomposes into 1-circuits (with only 0-cells in common) iff each vertex has even degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove necessity and sufficiency: show graphs consisting of disjoint cycles have even-degree vertices, and conversely group incident edges into pairs at each vertex to produce C' of cycles. Relate to known graph-theory theorems (Eulerian subgraph characterization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct C' by pairing incident edges and analyze dependence on pairing
rubrics_metrics.description: Given C1 where each vertex has even degree, group incident edges arbitrarily into pairs at each vertex to form a new graph C' whose vertices correspond to paired edges; C' consists of 1-circuits. The resulting C' depends on the pairing choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Veblen's construction to example graphs (G4, G5), show different pairings yield different sets of circuits, and provide counterexamples where C' circuits are not coincident with original C1 circuits for arbitrary pairings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic characterization of 1-circuits via H1·x ≡ 0 (mod 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A binary vector x (indicator for a set of edges) satisfies H1 x ≡ 0 (mod 2) iff the corresponding set of 1-cells forms a 1-circuit or system of 1-circuits (each vertex incident with an even number of chosen edges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret each row equation as parity of incident chosen edges at that vertex. Compute examples (e.g., for G3) with provided X and Y vectors to check whether they represent circuits. Emphasize reduction modulo 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null space basis yields complete set of 1-circuits
rubrics_metrics.description: If rank(H1)=r then there are α1 - r linearly independent (mod 2) solutions of H1 x = 0; these correspond to α1 - r 1-circuits or systems of circuits from which all others can be obtained by mod-2 addition. This is called a complete set of 1-circuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain equivalence between null space basis (over GF(2)) and a minimal generating set of circuits. For a given H1 (e.g., G6), find a null-space basis (mod 2), convert basis vectors to circuits, and express a given circuit as sum of basis circuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical matrix computations over GF(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform rank, null-space, and matrix-vector multiplications modulo 2 to analyze H1 and H0, determine linear relations among rows, and identify circuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out row/column reductions modulo 2 by hand as required (calculator matrix utilities may give incorrect results for mod-2 arithmetic). Use linear algebra concepts (rank, kernel, linear independence) appropriate to GF(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret algebraic results geometrically/topologically
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate linear-algebraic conclusions (e.g., nullspace solutions, row relations, block structure) back to geometric/topological properties of graphs (components, circuits, decomposition into cycles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deriving algebraic facts, explicitly state the geometric meaning (e.g., a row-sum relation corresponds to a component; a nullspace vector corresponds to collection of cycles). Use diagrams and labeled examples to support interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Turing's machine definitions in own words
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret Turing's definitions: 'machine', 'tape', 'scanned square', 'scanned symbol', 'm-configurations', 'configuration', 'automatic machine (a-machine)' and 'choice machine (c-machine)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paraphrase Turing's description, explain the role of finite memory (m-configurations), allowed operations (write, erase, move left/right, change m-configuration), and the distinction between deterministic automatic machines and non-deterministic choice machines. Relate to modern models where helpful.
